This module covers the Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2), the standard middleware for robotics development.

- ROS 2 architecture and concepts
- Nodes, topics, services, and actions
- URDF for humanoid robot description
- Python-to-ROS integration

ROS 2 is the communication backbone for every later module: simulation in Gazebo and Isaac Sim, perception pipelines and vision-language-action models all exchange data as ROS 2 messages. Over three weeks you move from single nodes to a complete humanoid description that can be visualized and driven from launch files. All examples use Python (`rclpy`) on ROS 2 Humble or Jazzy.

1. ROS 2 Architecture (Week 3): DDS and the rmw layer, QoS, nodes, executors, topics, the `ros2` CLI and custom messages
2. Services, Actions and Parameters (Week 4): request/response services, long-running actions with feedback and cancellation, and YAML-configured parameters
3. URDF, TF2 and Launch Files (Week 5): describing a humanoid with URDF and xacro, coordinate frames with TF2, `robot_state_publisher` and Python launch files
Complete Module 1: Introduction to Physical AI

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Describe the architecture of modern Gazebo (server, GUI, systems, transport)
2. Configure a physics engine, step size, and real-time factor for a simulation
3. Author an SDF world with a ground plane, lighting, and a simple model
4. Spawn a URDF robot into Gazebo from ROS 2 using `ros_gz_sim`

---

Before a humanoid takes its first real step, it takes thousands of simulated ones. Simulation lets you test controllers without risking hardware, reproduce bugs deterministically, and run experiments faster than real time. Gazebo is the open-source simulator most tightly integrated with ROS 2, and it is the workhorse for this module.

This chapter targets Gazebo Harmonic (an LTS release) paired with ROS 2 Jazzy Jalisco on Ubuntu 24.04, which is the officially recommended pairing. Commands use the modern `gz` CLI. If you use a different Gazebo release, plugin file names and some SDF tags may differ — check the release documentation.

The older simulator — now called Gazebo Classic (versions up to Gazebo 11, launched with the `gazebo` command) — reached end-of-life in January 2025. Many online tutorials still use Classic syntax such as `libgazebo_ros_camera.so` plugins or `gazebo_ros` packages. Those do not work with modern Gazebo. If a tutorial mentions `gazebo_ros_pkgs`, it is Classic.

The simplest route is to install the ROS-packaged Gazebo integration, which pulls in the matching Gazebo Harmonic libraries:

# Assumes ROS 2 Jazzy is already installed and sourced
sudo apt update
sudo apt install ros-jazzy-ros-gz

# Verify the simulator starts (opens the GUI with an example world)
gz sim shapes.sdf

The `ros-jazzy-ros-gz` metapackage includes `ros_gz_sim` (launching and spawning), `ros_gz_bridge` (topic bridging), and `ros_gz_image` (efficient image transport).

Modern Gazebo is a collection of libraries (`gz-sim`, `gz-physics`, `gz-sensors`, `gz-rendering`, `gz-transport`, `gz-msgs`, and `sdformat`) rather than a single monolithic program.

┌─────────────── gz sim ───────────────┐
│  Server: ECS + Systems (plugins)     │      ┌──────────────────┐
│   Physics │ Sensors │ UserCommands   │◄────►│  GUI (optional)  │
│   SceneBroadcaster │ ...             │      └──────────────────┘
└──────────────────┬───────────────────┘   gz-transport topics/services
                   ▼
            ros_gz_bridge  ◄──►  ROS 2 nodes

The server owns the simulation state and steps physics. The GUI is only a client that renders what the server broadcasts. They can run in one process or separately:

# Server + GUI together, start running immediately (-r)
gz sim -r my_world.sdf

# Server only (headless) — ideal for CI or remote machines
gz sim -s -r my_world.sdf

# GUI only, connecting to an already running server
gz sim -g

Internally, every object (world, model, link, joint, sensor) is an entity holding components (pose, mass, velocity, and so on). Behaviour is implemented by systems — plugins that read and write components each iteration. Physics, sensors, and even user commands from the GUI are all systems. If a system is not loaded, its feature simply does not exist: a world without the Sensors system produces no camera images.

`gz-transport` is a publish/subscribe and service middleware, similar in spirit to ROS 2 but independent from it. You can inspect it directly:

gz topic -l                        # list topics
gz topic -e -t /clock              # echo a topic
gz topic -i -t /world/demo/stats   # show publishers and message type

ROS 2 cannot see these topics directly — that is the job of `ros_gz_bridge`, covered in the next chapter.

chunks.section: Physics Engines, Step Size, and Real-Time Factor
chunks.text:
`gz-physics` is an abstraction with interchangeable engine plugins:

| Engine plugin | Typical use | Notes |
|---------------|-------------|-------|
| DART (`gz-physics-dartsim-plugin`) | General articulated robots | Default engine in Harmonic |
| Bullet Featherstone (`gz-physics-bullet-featherstone-plugin`) | Articulated bodies, many contacts | Reduced-coordinate articulations |
| TPE (`gz-physics-tpe-plugin`) | Large numbers of simple kinematic objects | Trivial Physics Engine: no dynamics, only basic collision checking |

Two parameters control time in every simulation:

- `max_step_size` — the physics time step in seconds. Smaller steps are more accurate and stable, but cost more computation per simulated second.
- `real_time_factor` (RTF) — the target ratio of simulated time to wall-clock time. A value of 1.0 means "try to run at real-time speed"; 0 means "run as fast as possible".

A third quantity, the achieved RTF, is what you actually get. If each step takes longer to compute than `max_step_size`, the simulation falls behind real time regardless of the target. The GUI shows the achieved RTF in the bottom-right corner.

chunks.section: Physics Engines, Step Size, and Real-Time Factor
chunks.text:
Legged robots have stiff contacts and fast balance loops. A step of 1 ms (`0.001`) is a common starting point. Make sure your controller rate is an integer divisor of the physics rate — for example, a 500 Hz controller on a 1 kHz physics loop — so that commands align with physics steps.

<physics name="1ms" type="ignored">
  <max_step_size>0.001</max_step_size>
  <real_time_factor>1.0</real_time_factor>
</physics>

<plugin filename="gz-sim-physics-system" name="gz::sim::systems::Physics">
  <engine>
    <filename>gz-physics-bullet-featherstone-plugin</filename>
  </engine>
</plugin>

The `type="ignored"` attribute is literal: Gazebo selects the engine through the Physics system plugin, not through the `type` attribute.

# Override the physics engine for one run
gz sim -r --physics-engine gz-physics-bullet-featherstone-plugin my_world.sdf

# Run headless and as fast as possible for batch experiments
# (set real_time_factor to 0 in the world file first)
gz sim -s -r --iterations 10000 my_world.sdf

SDF (Simulation Description Format) describes entire worlds: lights, models, physics settings, and plugins. URDF, which you met with ROS 2, describes only a single robot. Save the following as `humanoid_lab.sdf`:

<?xml version="1.0" ?>
<sdf version="1.10">
  <world name="humanoid_lab">

    <physics name="1ms" type="ignored">
      <max_step_size>0.001</max_step_size>
      <real_time_factor>1.0</real_time_factor>
    </physics>

    <!-- Core systems: physics, GUI commands, and state broadcasting -->
    <plugin filename="gz-sim-physics-system" name="gz::sim::systems::Physics"/>
    <plugin filename="gz-sim-user-commands-system" name="gz::sim::systems::UserCommands"/>
    <plugin filename="gz-sim-scene-broadcaster-system" name="gz::sim::systems::SceneBroadcaster"/>

    <gravity>0 0 -9.81</gravity>

    <light type="directional" name="sun">
      <cast_shadows>true</cast_shadows>
      <pose>0 0 10 0 0 0</pose>
      <diffuse>0.8 0.8 0.8 1</diffuse>
      <specular>0.2 0.2 0.2 1</specular>
      <direction>-0.5 0.1 -0.9</direction>
    </light>

<model name="ground_plane">
      <static>true</static>
      <link name="link">
        <collision name="collision">
          <geometry><plane><normal>0 0 1</normal><size>100 100</size></plane></geometry>
          <surface>
            <friction><ode><mu>1.0</mu><mu2>1.0</mu2></ode></friction>
          </surface>
        </collision>
        <visual name="visual">
          <geometry><plane><normal>0 0 1</normal><size>100 100</size></plane></geometry>
          <material><diffuse>0.7 0.7 0.7 1</diffuse></material>
        </visual>
      </link>
    </model>

    <!-- A 0.5 m box obstacle with explicit mass and inertia -->
    <model name="obstacle_box">
      <pose>2.0 0 0.25 0 0 0</pose>
      <link name="link">
        <inertial>
          <mass>5.0</mass>
          <inertia><ixx>0.2083</ixx><iyy>0.2083</iyy><izz>0.2083</izz></inertia>
        </inertial>
        <collision name="collision">
          <geometry><box><size>0.5 0.5 0.5</size></box></geometry>
        </collision>
        <visual name="visual">
          <geometry><box><size>0.5 0.5 0.5</size></box></geometry>
          <material><diffuse>0.8 0.2 0.2 1</diffuse></material>
        </visual>
      </link>
    </model>

  </world>
</sdf>

The box inertia follows the solid-cuboid formula: each diagonal term equals `m * (a² + b²) / 12`, which for a 5 kg, 0.5 m cube gives about 0.2083 kg·m². Run it with `gz sim -r humanoid_lab.sdf`. Always validate your files before debugging behaviour:

gz sdf -k humanoid_lab.sdf   # check the file for errors
gz sdf -p robot.urdf         # print the SDF that a URDF converts to

Your robot description from Module 2 is most likely URDF (often generated from Xacro). Gazebo converts URDF to SDF automatically when spawning. The robot must have an `<inertial>` block on every non-fixed link, and `<collision>` geometry wherever it should touch the world.

The `ros_gz_sim` package provides a `create` node that spawns a model from a file, from a string, or from the `robot_description` topic published by `robot_state_publisher`:

# Terminal 1: start Gazebo with the world
ros2 launch ros_gz_sim gz_sim.launch.py gz_args:="-r humanoid_lab.sdf"

# Terminal 2: spawn from a URDF file, 1 m above the ground
ros2 run ros_gz_sim create -world humanoid_lab -file my_humanoid.urdf \
    -name my_humanoid -x 0 -y 0 -z 1.0

Meshes referenced with `package://` URIs must be findable by Gazebo. Add your package's share directory's parent to `GZ_SIM_RESOURCE_PATH`, or install meshes so that the ROS-to-Gazebo path resolution in `ros_gz_sim` can locate them.

chunks.section: Putting It Together: A ros_gz_sim Launch File
chunks.text:
In practice you launch the simulator, the robot description, and the spawner together:

# launch/sim.launch.py

from ament_index_python.packages import get_package_share_directory
from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch.actions import IncludeLaunchDescription
from launch.launch_description_sources import PythonLaunchDescriptionSource
from launch_ros.actions import Node

def generate_launch_description():
    pkg_share = get_package_share_directory('my_humanoid_sim')
    ros_gz_sim_share = get_package_share_directory('ros_gz_sim')

    world = os.path.join(pkg_share, 'worlds', 'humanoid_lab.sdf')
    urdf_xacro = os.path.join(pkg_share, 'urdf', 'my_humanoid.urdf.xacro')
    robot_description = xacro.process_file(urdf_xacro).toxml()

    gazebo = IncludeLaunchDescription(
        PythonLaunchDescriptionSource(
            os.path.join(ros_gz_sim_share, 'launch', 'gz_sim.launch.py')),
        launch_arguments={'gz_args': f'-r {world}'}.items(),
    )

    robot_state_publisher = Node(
        package='robot_state_publisher',
        executable='robot_state_publisher',
        parameters=[{'robot_description': robot_description,
                     'use_sim_time': True}],
    )

chunks.section: Putting It Together: A ros_gz_sim Launch File

chunks.text:
- Mixing Classic and modern syntax: plugins named `libgazebo_ros_*.so` or tags from Gazebo Classic tutorials are silently ignored or rejected by `gz sim`.
- Missing systems: a world without the Physics, UserCommands, or SceneBroadcaster systems may load but appear frozen, or the GUI may show nothing. If you define any plugin in the world, Gazebo stops loading its default systems, so list all the ones you need.
- Links without inertia: URDF links with no `<inertial>` element are dropped or merged during conversion, and zero or tiny inertias cause explosions. Compute realistic values from CAD or geometric formulas.
- Robot spawned inside the ground: spawn with a positive `-z` offset so the feet start above the plane.
- Meshes not found: models appear invisible or without collisions; check `GZ_SIM_RESOURCE_PATH` and the console for resource-lookup errors.
- Low achieved RTF: very small step sizes, high-polygon collision meshes, and many contacts slow everything down. Use simple primitives for collisions and detailed meshes only for visuals.

- Modern Gazebo (Harmonic with ROS 2 Jazzy) replaces Gazebo Classic, which is end-of-life
- The server runs the simulation; the GUI is an optional client; features come from systems (plugins)
- `gz-transport` carries Gazebo's own topics and services, separate from ROS 2
- Step size trades accuracy for speed; real-time factor sets the target speed of simulated time
- SDF describes whole worlds; URDF robots are converted to SDF when spawned with `ros_gz_sim create`
- A launch file combining `gz_sim.launch.py`, `robot_state_publisher`, and the spawner is the standard entry point

In the next chapter, we add simulated sensors to the robot and bridge their data into ROS 2.

---

Exercise: Easy: Gazebo Architecture Check

Answer the following questions:

1. What is the difference between the Gazebo server and the GUI? Why is it useful that they can run separately?
2. What happens to the achieved real-time factor if one physics step takes longer to compute than `max_step_size`?
3. Name two signs that a tutorial you found online targets Gazebo Classic rather than modern Gazebo.

Exercise: Medium: Gazebo World with Obstacles. Reuse the obstacle_box model with different poses and names. Use the cylinder inertia formulas: ixx = iyy = m(3r² + h²)/12 and izz = mr²/2.

Extend `humanoid_lab.sdf` to include:

1. Three box obstacles and one cylinder obstacle at different positions, each with correct mass and inertia
2. A low ramp (a rotated static box) that a robot could walk up
3. A second physics configuration: run the world once with a 1 ms step and once with a 4 ms step, and record the achieved RTF shown in the GUI for each

Validate the file with `gz sdf -k` before running it.

Exercise: Challenging: Import Your Robot into Gazebo. Start with a two-link arm before trying a full humanoid. Use gz sdf -p on your URDF to see exactly what Gazebo receives.

Create a ROS 2 package `my_humanoid_sim` containing:

1. A URDF or Xacro description of a simple robot with at least three links, each with collision geometry and computed inertia
2. The `humanoid_lab.sdf` world in a `worlds/` folder, installed through `CMakeLists.txt` or `setup.py`
3. A launch file that starts Gazebo, `robot_state_publisher`, and spawns the robot

Document which physics engine you used and why, and report what happens when you deliberately remove the inertial block from one link.

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Add camera, depth camera, GPU LiDAR, IMU, and contact/force-torque sensors to an SDF model
2. Configure realistic noise models for simulated sensors
3. Bridge Gazebo sensor topics to ROS 2 with a `ros_gz_bridge` YAML configuration
4. Consume and visualise simulated sensor data with rclpy and RViz2
5. Evaluate when Unity is an appropriate alternative for rendering

---

In Module 1 you learned how real cameras, LiDARs, and IMUs work. In simulation, those sensors are replaced by software models that render images, cast rays, or read physics state. A perception or balance pipeline that works on perfect, noise-free data will almost certainly fail on hardware, so adding realistic noise is as important as adding the sensor itself.

As in the previous chapter, this chapter assumes Gazebo Harmonic with ROS 2 Jazzy, SDF 1.10, and the `ros-jazzy-ros-gz` packages.

Sensors in Gazebo are driven by systems that must be loaded in the world file. Rendering-based sensors (cameras, depth cameras, GPU LiDAR) share one system; physics-based sensors each have their own:

<!-- Add these inside <world>, alongside the Physics system -->
<plugin filename="gz-sim-sensors-system" name="gz::sim::systems::Sensors"><render_engine>ogre2</render_engine></plugin>
<plugin filename="gz-sim-imu-system" name="gz::sim::systems::Imu"/>
<plugin filename="gz-sim-contact-system" name="gz::sim::systems::Contact"/>
<plugin filename="gz-sim-forcetorque-system" name="gz::sim::systems::ForceTorque"/>

| Sensor | SDF `type` | Needs system | Needs GPU rendering | Default output message |
|--------|-----------|--------------|---------------------|------------------------|
| RGB camera | `camera` | Sensors | Yes | `gz.msgs.Image` |
| Depth camera | `depth_camera` | Sensors | Yes | `gz.msgs.Image` (float depth) |
| GPU LiDAR | `gpu_lidar` | Sensors | Yes | `gz.msgs.LaserScan`, plus `PointCloudPacked` on a `/points` topic |
| IMU | `imu` | Imu | No | `gz.msgs.IMU` |
| Contact | `contact` | Contact | No | `gz.msgs.Contacts` |
| Force-torque | `force_torque` | ForceTorque | No | `gz.msgs.Wrench` |

Sensors are attached to links (or, for force-torque, to joints). In URDF, wrap the SDF sensor block in a `<gazebo reference="link_name">` element so the converter attaches it to the correct link.

<sensor name="head_camera" type="camera">
  <pose>0.05 0 0 0 0 0</pose>
  <always_on>true</always_on>
  <update_rate>30</update_rate>
  <visualize>true</visualize>
  <topic>head_camera/image</topic>
  <gz_frame_id>head_camera_link</gz_frame_id>
  <camera>
    <horizontal_fov>1.047</horizontal_fov>
    <image><width>640</width><height>480</height><format>R8G8B8</format></image>
    <clip><near>0.05</near><far>50.0</far></clip>
    <noise><type>gaussian</type><mean>0.0</mean><stddev>0.007</stddev></noise>
  </camera>
</sensor>

Image noise is additive per pixel, with the standard deviation expressed on a 0–1 intensity scale. The camera also publishes calibration on a `camera_info` topic next to the image topic.

<sensor name="head_depth" type="depth_camera">
  <update_rate>15</update_rate>
  <topic>head_depth</topic>
  <gz_frame_id>head_camera_link</gz_frame_id>
  <camera>
    <horizontal_fov>1.047</horizontal_fov>
    <image><width>320</width><height>240</height><format>R_FLOAT32</format></image>
    <clip><near>0.1</near><far>8.0</far></clip>
    <noise><type>gaussian</type><mean>0.0</mean><stddev>0.01</stddev></noise>
  </camera>
</sensor>

Depth values are in metres. For combined colour and depth from one sensor, use the `rgbd_camera` type, which publishes image, depth image, and point cloud topics.

<sensor name="lidar" type="gpu_lidar">
  <pose>0 0 0.1 0 0 0</pose>
  <update_rate>10</update_rate>
  <topic>lidar</topic>
  <gz_frame_id>lidar_link</gz_frame_id>
  <lidar>
    <scan>
      <horizontal><samples>720</samples><resolution>1</resolution>
        <min_angle>-3.14159</min_angle><max_angle>3.14159</max_angle></horizontal>
      <vertical><samples>16</samples><resolution>1</resolution>
        <min_angle>-0.2618</min_angle><max_angle>0.2618</max_angle></vertical>
    </scan>
    <range><min>0.1</min><max>30.0</max><resolution>0.01</resolution></range>
    <noise><type>gaussian</type><mean>0.0</mean><stddev>0.01</stddev></noise>
  </lidar>
</sensor>

With one vertical sample this behaves like a 2D laser scanner; with several it approximates a multi-beam 3D LiDAR.

<sensor name="torso_imu" type="imu">
  <always_on>true</always_on>
  <update_rate>200</update_rate>
  <topic>imu</topic>
  <gz_frame_id>torso_link</gz_frame_id>
  <imu>
    <angular_velocity>
      <x><noise type="gaussian"><mean>0</mean><stddev>0.0002</stddev>
        <bias_mean>0.00001</bias_mean><bias_stddev>0.000001</bias_stddev></noise></x>
      <!-- y and z: identical noise blocks, omitted for brevity -->
    </angular_velocity>
    <linear_acceleration>
      <x><noise type="gaussian"><mean>0</mean><stddev>0.017</stddev></noise></x>
      <!-- y and z: identical noise blocks, omitted for brevity -->
    </linear_acceleration>
  </imu>
</sensor>

Bias terms model the slowly varying offset that causes drift when integrating a real IMU. Take noise values from your IMU's datasheet rather than guessing.

<!-- Contact sensor on the foot link: reports collisions of one collision element -->
<sensor name="left_foot_contact" type="contact">
  <update_rate>100</update_rate>
  <topic>left_foot/contact</topic>
  <contact><collision>left_foot_collision</collision></contact>
</sensor>

<!-- Force-torque sensor on the ankle JOINT (placed inside the joint element) -->
<sensor name="left_ankle_ft" type="force_torque">
  <update_rate>500</update_rate>
  <topic>left_ankle/wrench</topic>
  <force_torque><frame>child</frame><measure_direction>child_to_parent</measure_direction></force_torque>
</sensor>

The `collision` name must match the collision element name after URDF-to-SDF conversion, which may differ from the URDF name. Check it with `gz sdf -p`.

Gaussian noise is a first approximation only. Real sensors also exhibit motion blur, rolling shutter, exposure changes, missing LiDAR returns on glass or black surfaces, and IMU temperature drift. Chapter 3 shows how to randomize these effects further.

Gazebo publishes on `gz-transport`; ROS 2 nodes need ROS topics. `ros_gz_bridge` translates between the two. For more than a couple of topics, use a YAML configuration file:

# config/bridge.yaml
- ros_topic_name: "/clock"
  gz_topic_name: "/clock"
  ros_type_name: "rosgraph_msgs/msg/Clock"
  gz_type_name: "gz.msgs.Clock"
  direction: GZ_TO_ROS

- ros_topic_name: "/imu"
  gz_topic_name: "/imu"
  ros_type_name: "sensor_msgs/msg/Imu"
  gz_type_name: "gz.msgs.IMU"
  direction: GZ_TO_ROS

- ros_topic_name: "/scan"
  gz_topic_name: "/lidar"
  ros_type_name: "sensor_msgs/msg/LaserScan"
  gz_type_name: "gz.msgs.LaserScan"
  direction: GZ_TO_ROS

- ros_topic_name: "/points"
  gz_topic_name: "/lidar/points"
  ros_type_name: "sensor_msgs/msg/PointCloud2"
  gz_type_name: "gz.msgs.PointCloudPacked"
  direction: GZ_TO_ROS

# Run the bridge from the YAML file
ros2 run ros_gz_bridge parameter_bridge --ros-args -p config_file:=config/bridge.yaml

# Images are best bridged with ros_gz_image, which supports image_transport
ros2 run ros_gz_image image_bridge /head_camera/image

# Quick one-off bridge: TOPIC@ROS_TYPE[GZ_TYPE  ([ = Gazebo to ROS, ] = ROS to Gazebo, @ = both)
ros2 run ros_gz_bridge parameter_bridge /imu@sensor_msgs/msg/Imu[gz.msgs.IMU

Other pairs follow the same pattern, for example `sensor_msgs/msg/CameraInfo` with `gz.msgs.CameraInfo`, and `geometry_msgs/msg/Wrench` with `gz.msgs.Wrench`. Bridging `/clock` is what makes `use_sim_time: True` work. Without it, nodes using simulation time wait forever for a clock that never arrives.

Sensor topics are high-rate and loss-tolerant, so subscribe with the sensor-data QoS profile (best-effort reliability, small history):


from rclpy.node import Node
from rclpy.qos import qos_profile_sensor_data
from sensor_msgs.msg import Imu, LaserScan

class SimSensorMonitor(Node):
    """Monitors simulated IMU tilt and the nearest LiDAR obstacle."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__('sim_sensor_monitor')
        self.create_subscription(Imu, '/imu', self.on_imu, qos_profile_sensor_data)
        self.create_subscription(LaserScan, '/scan', self.on_scan, qos_profile_sensor_data)
        self.tilt_limit = math.radians(20.0)

    def on_imu(self, msg: Imu) -> None:
        a = msg.linear_acceleration
        roll = math.atan2(a.y, a.z)
        pitch = math.atan2(-a.x, math.sqrt(a.y  2 + a.z  2))
        if abs(roll) > self.tilt_limit or abs(pitch) > self.tilt_limit:
            self.get_logger().warn(
                f'Tilt warning: roll={math.degrees(roll):.1f} deg, '
                f'pitch={math.degrees(pitch):.1f} deg')

    def on_scan(self, msg: LaserScan) -> None:
        valid = [r for r in msg.ranges if msg.range_min <= r <= msg.range_max]
        if valid:
            self.get_logger().info(
                f'Nearest obstacle: {min(valid):.2f} m', throttle_duration_sec=1.0)

def main():
    rclpy.init()
    rclpy.spin(SimSensorMonitor())
    rclpy.shutdown()

if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

Run it with simulation time so its timestamps match the simulator: `ros2 run my_humanoid_sim sim_sensor_monitor --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true`.

RViz2 draws sensor data in 3D, but only if it can transform every message's `frame_id` into the chosen fixed frame. That transform tree comes from `robot_state_publisher` (which needs joint states) plus a transform from the world to the robot base. Start it with `rviz2 --ros-args -p use_sim_time:=true`, then:

1. Set Fixed Frame to your robot's base frame (for example `base_link`) to start.
2. Add a LaserScan display on `/scan` and a PointCloud2 display on `/points`.
3. Add an Image display on `/head_camera/image`, plus TF and RobotModel displays to confirm frames line up.

If a display shows "No transform from ... to ...", the `gz_frame_id` in the SDF does not match a frame in the TF tree, or joint states are not being published.

chunks.section: A Note on Unity as a Rendering Alternative
chunks.text:
Gazebo's renderer is adequate for most robotics work, but some teams want game-engine visuals — for example, to generate synthetic images for training vision models. Unity can be connected to ROS 2 through Unity's open-source Unity Robotics Hub projects:

- ROS-TCP-Connector — a Unity package that publishes and subscribes to ROS messages from C# scripts
- ROS-TCP-Endpoint — a ROS 2 node that relays those messages over TCP
- URDF Importer — imports a URDF robot as Unity `ArticulationBody` components

On the ROS 2 side you build ROS-TCP-Endpoint from source (its `main-ros2` branch) and run `ros2 run ros_tcp_endpoint default_server_endpoint --ros-args -p ROS_IP:=0.0.0.0`.

Be honest about the trade-offs. Unity uses its own physics (PhysX), so robot dynamics will not match Gazebo's. Messages cross a TCP relay instead of native DDS, and simulation time is not synchronised with ROS 2 automatically. The Unity Robotics repositories have seen limited updates in recent years, so verify compatibility with your Unity and ROS 2 versions before committing a project to them. For GPU-accelerated photorealism tightly integrated with robotics tooling, Module 4 covers NVIDIA Isaac Sim, which is the more common choice for that use case today.

- No sensor output at all: the Sensors, Imu, Contact, or ForceTorque system is missing from the world file.
- Rendering sensors fail on headless machines: cameras and GPU LiDAR need a working OpenGL context; on servers you may need a virtual display or EGL setup.
- Wrong frame IDs: without `gz_frame_id`, Gazebo uses a scoped name such as `model::link::sensor`, which does not match your TF tree.
- Mismatched bridge types: a typo in `gz_type_name` makes the bridge create nothing; check with `gz topic -i -t` which type is actually published. Likewise, forgetting to bridge `/clock` stalls every node using `use_sim_time`.
- QoS mismatches: a reliable subscription receives nothing from a best-effort publisher, and ROS 2 only logs a warning. A best-effort subscription such as `qos_profile_sensor_data` is compatible with both, which is why it is the safe default for sensor topics.
- Update rates too high: a 1 kHz camera will crush the achieved real-time factor. Match rates to the real hardware.

- Rendering sensors (camera, depth, GPU LiDAR) need the Sensors system; IMU, contact, and force-torque need their own systems
- Every sensor should carry a noise model based on real datasheets
- `ros_gz_bridge` with a YAML config maps Gazebo topics and types to ROS 2; always bridge `/clock`
- Subscribe with sensor-data QoS and run nodes with `use_sim_time`
- RViz2 needs a consistent TF tree and matching `gz_frame_id` values
- Unity is a possible rendering alternative, with real trade-offs in physics fidelity, time sync, and maintenance

In the next chapter, we tackle the hardest part of simulation: making behaviour learned in simulation survive contact with the real world.

---

Exercise: Easy: Sensor Simulation Concepts

Answer the following questions:

1. Which Gazebo system must be loaded for a `gpu_lidar` sensor, and which for an `imu` sensor?
2. What is the difference between the `mean`, `stddev`, and `bias_mean` terms in an IMU noise model?
3. Why does a node with `use_sim_time` enabled appear to hang when `/clock` is not bridged?

Exercise: Medium: Custom Sensor Suite. Add the sensors inside gazebo reference elements in your URDF, then write one bridge.yaml entry per topic. Use gz topic -l to confirm the Gazebo topic names before writing the YAML.

Add an RGB camera, a 2D LiDAR (one vertical sample), and an IMU to the robot from Chapter 3.1:

1. Give each sensor a noise model and a correct `gz_frame_id`
2. Write a `bridge.yaml` that bridges all three sensors plus `/clock`
3. Visualise all three in RViz2 with the TF and RobotModel displays enabled
4. Extend `SimSensorMonitor` to publish a `std_msgs/msg/Bool` on `/obstacle_close` when any LiDAR range is below 0.5 m

Exercise: Challenging: Foot Contact Estimator. Contact messages are only published while contact exists, so treat a timeout as no contact. For force-torque, a vertical force threshold with hysteresis avoids flickering.

For a biped (or a simple two-legged test model):

1. Add a contact sensor to each foot and a force-torque sensor to each ankle joint
2. Bridge both to ROS 2 (use `ros_gz_interfaces/msg/Contacts` for contacts)
3. Write an rclpy node that estimates the gait phase (left stance, right stance, double support, flight) from the sensors
4. Compare the contact-based and force-based estimates while the robot is pushed around with the GUI, and explain any disagreement

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Identify the main sources of the reality gap between simulation and hardware
2. Implement physics, visual, and sensor-noise domain randomization
3. Apply system identification to fit simulation parameters to real data
4. Model actuator limits and control latency in simulation
5. Apply a structured validation checklist before running a controller on real hardware

---

A controller that walks perfectly in Gazebo may fall over on its first real step. The difference between the simulated world and the physical one is called the reality gap. It cannot be eliminated — every simulator is an approximation — but it can be narrowed (make the simulator more accurate) and bridged (make the controller robust to whatever inaccuracy remains). Good sim-to-real practice does both.

Code in this chapter is plain Python (NumPy and SciPy) so that it applies to any simulator, including Gazebo from the previous chapters and Isaac Sim in Module 4. Numeric ranges shown are illustrative starting points, not measured values for any particular robot — always derive yours from your own hardware and datasheets.

| Source | Simulation assumption | Real-world behaviour |
|--------|----------------------|---------------------|
| Rigid-body parameters | Masses and inertias from CAD | Cables, fasteners, and batteries change mass distribution |
| Contact and friction | Simplified friction cone, rigid contacts | Friction varies by surface, wear, and dust; feet deform |
| Actuators | Ideal torque sources | Torque limits, gearbox friction, backlash, heating, bandwidth limits |
| Latency | Commands applied instantly | Communication, computation, and driver delays of several milliseconds |
| Sensors | Gaussian noise at best | Bias drift, dropouts, motion blur, timestamp jitter |
| Rendering | Clean textures, ideal lighting | Glare, shadows, reflections, changing illumination |
| Environment | Flat, known ground | Uneven floors, compliant carpets, unexpected obstacles |

For humanoids, the actuator, latency, and contact rows usually dominate, because balance depends on applying the right force at the right time through the feet.

Domain randomization trains or tunes a controller across many randomly varied simulations, so that the real world looks like just another sample from the training distribution. It was popularised for vision by Tobin et al. (2017, "Domain Randomization for Transferring Deep Neural Networks from Simulation to the Real World") and for dynamics by Peng et al. (2018, "Sim-to-Real Transfer of Robotic Control with Dynamics Randomization").

The key design decision is the range of each parameter. Too narrow and the controller overfits to the simulator; too wide and it becomes overly conservative or fails to learn at all.

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class PhysicsSample:
    """One randomized set of physics parameters for an episode."""
    mass_scale: np.ndarray       # per-link multiplier
    com_offset: np.ndarray       # per-link centre-of-mass shift (m), shape (N, 3)
    ground_friction: float
    joint_damping_scale: np.ndarray
    motor_strength_scale: np.ndarray

class PhysicsRandomizer:
    """Samples physics parameters around nominal values."""

    def __init__(self, n_links: int, n_joints: int, seed: int | None = None):
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.n_links = n_links
        self.n_joints = n_joints

def sample(self) -> dict:
        return {
            "light_direction": self.rng.normal([-0.5, 0.1, -0.9], 0.2).tolist(),
            "light_intensity": float(self.rng.uniform(0.4, 1.2)),
            "floor_texture": str(self.rng.choice(self.textures)),
            "floor_rgb": self.rng.uniform(0.2, 0.9, 3).tolist(),
            # Small camera mounting errors (rad) mimic imperfect calibration
            "camera_rpy_offset": self.rng.normal(0.0, 0.01, 3).tolist(),
            "camera_fov_scale": float(self.rng.uniform(0.97, 1.03)),
        }

Visual randomization matters most for learned perception. Classical geometric pipelines are usually more sensitive to calibration errors than to textures.


class IMUNoiseModel:
    """White noise plus a random-walk bias, re-sampled per episode."""

    def __init__(self, dt: float, seed: int | None = None):
        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.dt = dt
        self.reset()

    def reset(self) -> None:
        # Randomize the noise level itself between episodes
        self.gyro_sigma = self.rng.uniform(1e-4, 5e-4)
        self.gyro_bias_walk = self.rng.uniform(1e-6, 1e-5)
        self.gyro_bias = self.rng.normal(0.0, 0.005, 3)
        self.dropout_prob = self.rng.uniform(0.0, 0.01)
        self.last_output = np.zeros(3)

def apply(self, true_gyro: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        self.gyro_bias += self.rng.normal(0.0, self.gyro_bias_walk * np.sqrt(self.dt), 3)
        if self.rng.random() < self.dropout_prob:
            return self.last_output          # stale sample, like a missed packet
        out = true_gyro + self.gyro_bias + self.rng.normal(0.0, self.gyro_sigma, 3)
        self.last_output = out
        return out

Unlike the fixed SDF noise from the previous chapter, this model varies the noise parameters themselves, so the controller cannot tune itself to one specific noise level.

Randomization bridges the gap; system identification narrows it. The idea is to record real robot data, then adjust simulation parameters until the simulated response matches. Start with the parts that matter most: joint friction, damping, and actuator response.

The example below fits viscous damping and Coulomb friction for a single joint, given a logged step response from hardware:


from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp
from scipy.optimize import least_squares

def simulate_joint(params, t, torque, inertia):
    """Single joint: I*qdd = tau - b*qd - fc*sign(qd)."""
    b, fc = params

    def dynamics(ti, x):
        q, qd = x
        tau = np.interp(ti, t, torque)
        qdd = (tau - b  qd - fc  np.tanh(qd / 0.01)) / inertia  # smooth sign()
        return [qd, qdd]

    sol = solve_ivp(dynamics, (t[0], t[-1]), [0.0, 0.0], t_eval=t, max_step=1e-3)
    return sol.y[1]  # joint velocity

def identify_friction(t, torque, measured_velocity, inertia):
    def residual(params):
        return simulate_joint(params, t, torque, inertia) - measured_velocity

    result = least_squares(residual, x0=[0.1, 0.1], bounds=([0.0, 0.0], [10.0, 10.0]))
    return {"viscous_damping": result.x[0], "coulomb_friction": result.x[1],
            "rmse": float(np.sqrt(np.mean(result.fun  2)))}

Good identification practice:

- Use several excitation signals (steps, chirps, slow ramps), not one trajectory
- Hold out part of the data and check that the fitted model predicts it
- Identify with the robot suspended first (no contacts), then on the ground
- Feed the identified values back into the URDF `<dynamics>` tags and centre your randomization ranges on them

Measure the real end-to-end latency (sensor timestamp to motor response), then randomize the delay around it — for instance by sampling `delay_steps` per episode. Hwangbo et al. (2019, "Learning Agile and Dynamic Motor Skills for Legged Robots") went further and trained a neural network on real actuator data to replace the analytic model; that is worth considering once a simple model is not enough.

- Version everything: world files, URDF, noise parameters, and randomization ranges belong in Git with the controller code.
- Seed your randomness so a failure seen in simulation can be reproduced exactly.
- Match rates and interfaces: run the controller in simulation at the same frequency, with the same message types, as on hardware. The code that ships should be the code that was simulated.
- Test headless in CI: a short `gz sim -s` regression run catches broken models before anyone reaches the lab.
- Log both worlds identically: record the same topics in simulation and on hardware (for example with `ros2 bag record`) so you can compare them side by side.
- Stress-test deliberately: apply pushes, drop sensor packets, and lower friction in simulation to find failure margins before hardware does.

chunks.section: Validation Checklist: Sim to Humanoid Hardware
chunks.text:
Work through these stages in order. Do not move to the next stage until the current one passes.

1. Simulation robustness
   - [ ] Controller succeeds across the full randomization range, not only nominal parameters
   - [ ] Latency and actuator models use measured values from the real robot
   - [ ] Failure cases are understood and documented
2. Interface check (robot powered, motors disabled)
   - [ ] Every sensor topic arrives at the expected rate, frame, and sign convention
   - [ ] Joint directions, zero offsets, and limits match the URDF
   - [ ] Emergency stop tested and reachable by the operator
3. Suspended test (robot on a gantry or harness)
   - [ ] Low-gain joint tracking compared against simulation with identical commands
   - [ ] Torque, velocity, and temperature limits enforced in software
4. Supported ground test
   - [ ] Standing balance with harness slack, then small perturbations
   - [ ] Logged data compared with simulation; large discrepancies trigger re-identification
5. Free operation
   - [ ] Clear area, spotter present, gradually increasing task difficulty

Humanoids are heavy, can fall suddenly, and have joints capable of injuring people. Follow your lab's safety procedures, keep a physical emergency stop within reach, and never test a new controller without a harness or spotter.

- Randomizing everything, widely: overly wide ranges produce timid controllers or prevent learning; start narrow, widen only where hardware tests show sensitivity.
- Randomizing around wrong nominal values: if the nominal mass is wrong by a large margin, randomization hides the error instead of fixing it — identify first.
- Ignoring latency: a controller tuned without delay often oscillates on hardware.
- Different code paths: a "simulation-only" shortcut in the controller means the tested code is not the deployed code.
- Trusting a single successful run: evaluate over many seeds and report the failure rate, not the best episode.

- The reality gap comes from dynamics, contacts, actuators, latency, sensors, and rendering
- Domain randomization makes controllers robust by training across varied physics, visuals, and noise
- System identification narrows the gap by fitting simulation parameters to real data
- Explicit actuator and latency models address the most common humanoid failure modes
- A staged validation checklist — simulation, interface, suspended, supported, free — manages risk when moving to hardware

Module 4 introduces NVIDIA Isaac, where GPU-parallel simulation makes large-scale domain randomization practical.

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
In Module 3 you simulated robots in Gazebo. Gazebo is an excellent general-purpose simulator, but humanoid development increasingly relies on three things it was not primarily built for: photorealistic rendering for training perception models, GPU-parallel physics for reinforcement learning, and large, composable scenes that many engineers edit at once.

NVIDIA Isaac Sim targets exactly these needs. It is a robotics simulator built on NVIDIA Omniverse, and every scene it loads is described in Universal Scene Description (USD), the open scene format originally developed by Pixar. Learning Isaac Sim is therefore really two skills: understanding USD as a data model, and understanding Isaac Sim's Python APIs for physics, sensors, and robots.

This chapter targets Isaac Sim 4.x (4.0 to 4.2) and its `omni.isaac.core` Python API. Isaac Sim is a fast-moving product: APIs, asset paths, and installation methods change between releases. Always check the official Isaac Sim documentation for the release you have installed.

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text: Starting with Isaac Sim 4.5, most Python modules were renamed. For example, `omni.isaac.core` became `isaacsim.core.api`, `omni.isaac.kit.SimulationApp` became `isaacsim.SimulationApp`, and the ROS 2 bridge extension `omni.isaac.ros2_bridge` became `isaacsim.ros2.bridge`. The concepts in this chapter are unchanged; only the import paths differ. If you use 4.5 or newer, consult the release's migration guide and adjust the imports.

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
Isaac Sim is an Omniverse Kit application. Kit is a plugin-based runtime in which nearly every feature ships as an extension. Isaac Sim is a curated bundle of those extensions plus robotics-specific ones.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        Isaac Sim (Kit app)                      │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Robotics extensions                                            │
│  ┌─────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌──────────┐ │
│  │ Core API    │ │ Sensors      │ │ ROS 2 bridge│ │Replicator│ │
│  │ (World,     │ │ (camera,     │ │ (OmniGraph  │ │(synthetic│ │
│  │ articulation│ │  lidar, IMU) │ │  nodes)     │ │  data)   │ │
│  └─────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └─────────────┘ └──────────┘ │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Omniverse Kit runtime: extension manager, OmniGraph, UI       │
├───────────────────────┬──────────────────┬─────────────────────┤
│  USD stage (OpenUSD)  │  PhysX (physics) │  RTX renderer       │
└───────────────────────┴──────────────────┴─────────────────────┘

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
| Layer | Responsibility |
|-------|----------------|
| USD stage | Holds the entire scene: geometry, materials, physics properties, robots, sensors |
| PhysX | Rigid body, articulation, and contact simulation, with GPU acceleration available |
| RTX renderer | Ray-traced and path-traced rendering for cameras and RTX-based lidar |
| OmniGraph | Visual and scriptable dataflow graphs, used heavily for ROS 2 publishing |
| Core API | Pythonic wrappers (`World`, `Articulation`, `XFormPrim`) around USD and PhysX |

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
Isaac Sim requires an NVIDIA RTX-class GPU with a recent driver, plenty of system memory, and fast storage. Exact minimum and recommended specifications change with every release, so check NVIDIA's current Isaac Sim requirements page before buying or provisioning hardware. Cloud GPU instances are a practical alternative when local hardware is insufficient.

In the 4.x series there are two common ways to install:

- Workstation install: download the packaged release and run scripts with the bundled `python.sh` (Linux) or `python.bat` (Windows).
- pip install: install the `isaacsim` packages from NVIDIA's package index into a Python environment that matches the release's required Python version.

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
USD is best understood as a layered, non-destructive database of scene description. Five concepts matter most.

| Concept | What it is | Robotics example |
|---------|-----------|------------------|
| Stage | The composed view of the scene you are working with | The full warehouse with robot, shelves, and lights |
| Prim | A named node in the scene hierarchy, addressed by a path | `/World/H1/pelvis` |
| Attribute | A typed, possibly time-sampled value on a prim | A joint's drive stiffness, a mesh's points |
| Layer | A file (`.usd`, `.usda`, `.usdc`) contributing opinions to the stage | `lighting.usda` owned by one engineer |
| Reference | Pulls another file's prim hierarchy into this stage | Inserting `h1.usd` under `/World/H1` |
| Variant set | Named alternatives on a prim, one selected at a time | Gripper variant: `parallel` or `suction` |

Composition is the rule system that merges layers, references, and variants into the final stage. Stronger layers override weaker ones, which lets a tester change a robot's mass in their own layer without touching the original robot file.

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
The `pxr` module is USD's Python API. It is available inside Isaac Sim's Python environment and also via the standalone `usd-core` package on PyPI, so you can practice these examples without a GPU.

from pxr import Usd, UsdGeom, UsdPhysics, Gf, Sdf

# Create a new stage backed by a human-readable .usda file
stage = Usd.Stage.CreateNew("warehouse.usda")
UsdGeom.SetStageUpAxis(stage, UsdGeom.Tokens.z)   # Isaac Sim uses Z-up
UsdGeom.SetStageMetersPerUnit(stage, 1.0)         # 1 unit = 1 meter

# Root transform, set as the default prim so references can target it
world = UsdGeom.Xform.Define(stage, "/World")
stage.SetDefaultPrim(world.GetPrim())

# A static shelf: a cube scaled into a box, with a collider
shelf = UsdGeom.Cube.Define(stage, "/World/Shelf")
shelf.GetSizeAttr().Set(1.0)
xform = UsdGeom.XformCommonAPI(shelf)
xform.SetTranslate(Gf.Vec3d(2.0, 0.0, 1.0))
xform.SetScale(Gf.Vec3f(0.5, 2.0, 2.0))
UsdPhysics.CollisionAPI.Apply(shelf.GetPrim())

# A dynamic box the robot might pick up: collider + rigid body + mass
box = UsdGeom.Cube.Define(stage, "/World/Box")
box.GetSizeAttr().Set(0.3)
UsdGeom.XformCommonAPI(box).SetTranslate(Gf.Vec3d(1.0, 0.5, 0.15))
UsdPhysics.CollisionAPI.Apply(box.GetPrim())
UsdPhysics.RigidBodyAPI.Apply(box.GetPrim())
UsdPhysics.MassAPI.Apply(box.GetPrim()).CreateMassAttr(2.0)

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
# A custom attribute for downstream tools (e.g. a task label)
box.GetPrim().CreateAttribute("task:label", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.String).Set("pick_target")

stage.GetRootLayer().Save()

Because `warehouse.usda` is plain text, you can open it in any editor, diff it, and review it like code. Binary `.usdc` files hold the same data in a more compact, faster-loading form.

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
The real power of USD shows up when several files cooperate. The tabs below show the three composition tools you will use most often.

    Sublayers stack opinions. Edits go to the current edit target, so each team member can own a layer.

        from pxr import Usd, Sdf, UsdGeom, Gf

    stage = Usd.Stage.Open("warehouse.usda")

    # Create a separate layer for lighting and add it as a sublayer
    lighting = Sdf.Layer.CreateNew("lighting.usda")
    stage.GetRootLayer().subLayerPaths.append("lighting.usda")

    # Direct new edits into the lighting layer
    stage.SetEditTarget(Usd.EditTarget(lighting))
    light = stage.DefinePrim("/World/KeyLight", "DistantLight")
    light.CreateAttribute("inputs:intensity", Sdf.ValueTypeNames.Float).Set(3000.0)

    lighting.Save()
    stage.GetRootLayer().Save()
    
    References bring in another asset, such as a robot, under a new path. The original file is never modified.

        from pxr import Usd, UsdGeom, Gf

    stage = Usd.Stage.Open("warehouse.usda")

    # Reference a robot asset (local path or Nucleus/HTTP URL)
    robot = stage.DefinePrim("/World/Robot", "Xform")
    robot.GetReferences().AddReference("./assets/humanoid.usd")

    # Local override: move the referenced robot without editing its file
    UsdGeom.XformCommonAPI(robot).SetTranslate(Gf.Vec3d(0.0, 0.0, 1.05))

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
stage.GetRootLayer().Save()
    
    Variant sets store alternatives on one prim. Only the selected variant is composed.

        from pxr import Usd, UsdGeom

    stage = Usd.Stage.Open("warehouse.usda")

    # A new prim whose size is authored ONLY inside the variants
    obstacle = UsdGeom.Cube.Define(stage, "/World/Obstacle")
    vset = obstacle.GetPrim().GetVariantSets().AddVariantSet("size")
    for name, edge in [("small", 0.2), ("large", 0.5)]:
        vset.AddVariant(name)
        vset.SetVariantSelection(name)
        with vset.GetVariantEditContext():
            obstacle.GetSizeAttr().Set(edge)

    vset.SetVariantSelection("small")      # choose the active variant
    print(obstacle.GetSizeAttr().Get())    # 0.2
    stage.GetRootLayer().Save()
    
    Local opinions are stronger than variant opinions. If the prim also had a size authored outside the variant set, that local value would win and switching variants would appear to do nothing.

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
Isaac Sim can be driven interactively through its GUI, through the Script Editor, or as a standalone Python application. Standalone scripts are the preferred workflow for reproducible experiments, CI jobs, and headless training runs.

The one rule that surprises newcomers: `SimulationApp` must be created before any other Omniverse import. Creating it boots the Kit runtime, and the other `omni.*` modules only exist after that.

# run with: ./python.sh humanoid_hello.py   (from the Isaac Sim install folder)
from omni.isaac.kit import SimulationApp

# 1. Boot Kit FIRST. headless=True skips the GUI window.
simulation_app = SimulationApp({"headless": False, "width": 1280, "height": 720})

# 2. Only now import the rest of the Isaac Sim API

from omni.isaac.core import World
from omni.isaac.core.articulations import Articulation
from omni.isaac.core.utils.stage import add_reference_to_stage
from omni.isaac.core.utils.nucleus import get_assets_root_path
from omni.isaac.core.utils.types import ArticulationAction

# 3. Build the world: physics + rendering step at fixed rates
world = World(stage_units_in_meters=1.0, physics_dt=1.0 / 200.0, rendering_dt=1.0 / 50.0)
world.scene.add_default_ground_plane()

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
# 4. Reference a robot asset. The exact path depends on your Isaac Sim
#    version; browse the Isaac assets in the GUI to confirm it.
assets_root = get_assets_root_path()
robot_usd = assets_root + "/Isaac/Robots/Unitree/H1/h1.usd"
add_reference_to_stage(usd_path=robot_usd, prim_path="/World/H1")

robot = world.scene.add(
    Articulation(prim_path="/World/H1", name="h1", position=np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.05]))
)

# 5. reset() initializes physics handles; call it before reading joint state
world.reset()
print(f"{robot.num_dof} DOF: {robot.dof_names}")

default_pose = robot.get_joint_positions()
controller = robot.get_articulation_controller()

# 6. Main loop: gently oscillate every joint around its default position
for step in range(2000):
    t = step * world.get_physics_dt()
    targets = default_pose + 0.1  np.sin(2.0  np.pi  0.5  t)
    controller.apply_action(ArticulationAction(joint_positions=targets))
    world.step(render=True)

simulation_app.close()

A few details are worth noticing:

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
- `physics_dt` versus `rendering_dt`: physics is stepped several times per rendered frame. Legged robots usually need a small physics step for stable contacts.
- Position targets, not positions: `joint_positions` in an `ArticulationAction` are targets for the joint drives. How closely the robot tracks them depends on the drive stiffness and damping authored in the USD file.
- The robot will likely fall. Nothing in this script balances the humanoid. That is the subject of Chapter 3.

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.section: Reading and Modifying USD from Isaac Sim
chunks.text:
Because Isaac Sim's scene is a USD stage, you can mix the Core API with raw `pxr` calls:


from pxr import UsdPhysics

stage = omni.usd.get_context().get_stage()

# List every revolute joint in the robot and read its drive stiffness
for prim in stage.Traverse():
    if not prim.GetPath().HasPrefix("/World/H1"):
        continue
    if prim.IsA(UsdPhysics.RevoluteJoint):
        drive = UsdPhysics.DriveAPI.Get(prim, "angular")
        stiffness = drive.GetStiffnessAttr().Get() if drive else None
        print(f"{prim.GetPath()}  stiffness={stiffness}")

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
| Aspect | Gazebo (Module 3) | Isaac Sim |
|--------|-------------------|-----------|
| Scene format | SDF / URDF | USD (URDF and MJCF can be imported) |
| Physics | Several engines (DART, Bullet, others) | NVIDIA PhysX, with GPU acceleration |
| Rendering | Rasterized (OGRE) | RTX ray tracing and path tracing |
| GPU requirement | Not required | NVIDIA RTX-class GPU required |
| ROS 2 integration | `ros_gz` bridge | ROS 2 bridge extension via OmniGraph |
| Synthetic data | Limited, custom plugins | Replicator with built-in annotators |

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
- **Importing `omni.*` before `SimulationApp`. You will see `ModuleNotFoundError` or strange extension errors. Always create `SimulationApp` first.
- Mixing 4.x and 4.5+ tutorials. Code using `isaacsim.core.api` will not run on 4.2, and vice versa. Check which release a tutorial targets.
- Forgetting `world.reset()`. Articulation handles are not valid until the world has been reset at least once.
- Wrong units or up axis. Assets authored in centimeters or Y-up will appear tiny or sideways. Check `metersPerUnit` and `upAxis` on the stage.
- Editing the wrong layer. Changes land on the current edit target. If a change "disappears" after reload, it was probably written to the session layer instead of the file you saved.
- Hard-coded asset paths. Asset locations move between releases; resolve them via `get_assets_root_path()` and verify in the asset browser.

chunks.page: Isaac Sim and Universal Scene Description
chunks.text:
- Isaac Sim is an Omniverse Kit application combining a USD stage, PhysX physics, RTX rendering, and robotics extensions
- USD describes scenes as composed layers of prims and attributes, with references and variants enabling reuse without copying
- The `pxr` API lets you author and inspect USD programmatically, inside or outside Isaac Sim
- Standalone scripts start with `SimulationApp`, then build a `World`, add articulations, call `reset()`, and step the simulation
- Isaac Sim's Python API changed names in 4.5; always match code to your installed release

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Explain how Isaac ROS and NITROS accelerate ROS 2 perception on NVIDIA GPUs
2. Configure and launch Isaac ROS Visual SLAM (cuVSLAM) with stereo and IMU input
3. Describe how nvblox builds 3D reconstructions and costmaps for navigation
4. Publish simulated sensor data from Isaac Sim to ROS 2 through the ROS 2 bridge
5. Generate labeled synthetic datasets with Omniverse Replicator

---

A humanoid walking through a building must answer two questions continuously: where am I? and what is around me? Answering them requires processing multiple camera streams, depth data, and IMU readings with low latency, on a computer that fits inside the robot.

Isaac ROS is NVIDIA's collection of GPU-accelerated ROS 2 packages built for this job. They run on NVIDIA Jetson modules and on desktop GPUs, and they plug into a standard ROS 2 graph, so they can be mixed with any other ROS 2 node you have written in Module 2.

Examples in this chapter assume Isaac ROS 3.x on ROS 2 Humble, typically run inside NVIDIA's Isaac ROS development container. Isaac ROS releases track specific ROS 2 distributions and JetPack versions, and parameter and topic names have changed between releases. Before copying a launch file, compare it with the documentation for the exact release you installed.

A conventional ROS 2 pipeline copies each image from GPU to CPU, serializes it into a message, and copies it back to the GPU in the next node. For high-resolution stereo streams these copies can dominate the pipeline's latency.

NITROS (NVIDIA Isaac Transport for ROS) removes that overhead. It builds on two ROS 2 Humble features:

- Type adaptation (REP 2007): a node can publish a custom in-memory type, such as a GPU buffer, and ROS 2 converts it to a standard message only when a subscriber actually needs one.
- Type negotiation (REP 2009): connected nodes agree on the most efficient shared format.

When two NITROS-enabled nodes run as composable nodes in the same process, image data can stay in GPU memory across the whole chain instead of making a GPU to CPU to GPU round trip at every hop.

The zero-copy benefit only applies between NITROS-enabled nodes in the same component container. A regular `rclpy` or `rclcpp` subscriber still receives a normal ROS 2 message, which forces a conversion. Design pipelines so the heavy GPU stages sit next to each other.

| Package | Purpose | Typical inputs | Typical outputs |
|---------|---------|----------------|-----------------|
| `isaac_ros_visual_slam` | Stereo visual-inertial odometry and SLAM (cuVSLAM) | Stereo images, camera info, IMU | Odometry, TF, SLAM path |
| `nvblox_ros` | GPU 3D reconstruction and ESDF | Depth or 3D lidar, color, pose | Mesh, ESDF, 2D costmap slice |
| `isaac_ros_image_proc` | Rectification, resize, format conversion | Raw images | Rectified images |
| `isaac_ros_dnn_inference` | TensorRT and Triton inference | Tensors | Tensors |

Isaac ROS Visual SLAM wraps NVIDIA's cuVSLAM library. It tracks visual features across stereo image pairs to estimate camera motion (visual odometry) and, optionally, fuses IMU data and builds a map with loop closure.

For a humanoid, visual-inertial odometry is especially valuable: walking produces large, jerky head motion, and the IMU helps the tracker through fast rotations and brief moments of poor visual texture.

Isaac ROS nodes are shipped as composable nodes. The launch file below loads cuVSLAM into a multithreaded component container.

# launch/humanoid_vslam.launch.py
from launch import LaunchDescription
from launch.actions import DeclareLaunchArgument
from launch.substitutions import LaunchConfiguration
from launch_ros.actions import ComposableNodeContainer
from launch_ros.descriptions import ComposableNode

def generate_launch_description():
    use_sim_time = LaunchConfiguration("use_sim_time")

visual_slam = ComposableNode(
        package="isaac_ros_visual_slam",
        plugin="nvidia::isaac_ros::visual_slam::VisualSlamNode",
        name="visual_slam_node",
        parameters=[{
            "use_sim_time": use_sim_time,
            "num_cameras": 2,                 # one stereo pair
            "rectified_images": True,
            "enable_imu_fusion": True,
            # add gyro/accel noise parameters from your IMU datasheet here
            "base_frame": "base_link",
            "odom_frame": "odom",
            "map_frame": "map",
            "imu_frame": "imu_link",
            "enable_slam_visualization": True,
        }],
        remappings=[
            ("visual_slam/image_0", "/head_camera/left/image_rect"),
            ("visual_slam/camera_info_0", "/head_camera/left/camera_info"),
            ("visual_slam/image_1", "/head_camera/right/image_rect"),
            ("visual_slam/camera_info_1", "/head_camera/right/camera_info"),
            ("visual_slam/imu", "/imu/data"),
        ],
    )

    container = ComposableNodeContainer(
        name="perception_container",
        namespace="",
        package="rclcpp_components",
        executable="component_container_mt",
        composable_node_descriptions=[visual_slam],
        output="screen",
    )

return LaunchDescription([
        DeclareLaunchArgument("use_sim_time", default_value="true"),
        container,
    ])

/head_camera/left/image_rect ─┐
/head_camera/left/camera_info ┤
/head_camera/right/image_rect ┼──> visual_slam_node ──> /visual_slam/tracking/odometry
/head_camera/right/camera_info┤         │           ──> /visual_slam/tracking/slam_path
/imu/data ────────────────────┘         │           ──> /visual_slam/status
                                        └──> TF: map → odom → base_link

Confirm that inputs arrive at the expected rate and that odometry is being produced.

Visual SLAM tells the robot where it is. nvblox tells it what the world looks like. It fuses depth images (or 3D lidar scans) with the robot's pose into a voxel grid on the GPU, producing:

- a TSDF (truncated signed distance field) used to extract a surface mesh for visualization
- an ESDF (Euclidean signed distance field) giving the distance to the nearest obstacle for any point
- a 2D costmap slice of the ESDF, which Nav2 can consume through an nvblox costmap layer

# Added to the same container as visual_slam_node
nvblox = ComposableNode(
    package="nvblox_ros",
    plugin="nvblox::NvbloxNode",
    name="nvblox_node",
    parameters=[{
        "use_sim_time": True,
        "global_frame": "odom",       # pose comes from TF published by VSLAM
        "voxel_size": 0.05,           # meters; smaller = more detail, more GPU memory
    }],
    remappings=[
        ("camera_0/depth/image", "/head_camera/depth/image_rect_raw"),
        ("camera_0/depth/camera_info", "/head_camera/depth/camera_info"),
        ("camera_0/color/image", "/head_camera/color/image_raw"),
        ("camera_0/color/camera_info", "/head_camera/color/camera_info"),
    ],
)

For a humanoid, the choice of height band for the 2D slice matters: it should cover everything between the floor and the top of the robot's head, otherwise overhanging obstacles such as tables will be invisible to the planner.

Perception models need labeled data, and labeling real images by hand is slow. Omniverse Replicator generates images together with ground-truth annotations (bounding boxes, segmentation masks, depth) directly from the simulator, while randomizing poses, lighting, and materials so the model does not overfit to one scene. This practice is called domain randomization.

from omni.isaac.kit import SimulationApp
simulation_app = SimulationApp({"headless": True})

with rep.new_layer():
    camera = rep.create.camera(position=(0, -4, 2), look_at=(0, 0, 0.5))
    render_product = rep.create.render_product(camera, (1024, 768))

    rep.create.plane(scale=10)
    boxes = rep.create.cube(count=8, scale=0.3, semantics=[("class", "box")])
    light = rep.create.light(light_type="Sphere", position=(2, -2, 4))

    # Re-randomize the scene on every generated frame
    with rep.trigger.on_frame(num_frames=200):
        with boxes:
            rep.modify.pose(
                position=rep.distribution.uniform((-2, -2, 0.15), (2, 2, 0.15)),
                rotation=rep.distribution.uniform((0, 0, -180), (0, 0, 180)),
            )
        with light:
            rep.modify.attribute("intensity", rep.distribution.uniform(5000, 30000))

writer = rep.WriterRegistry.get("BasicWriter")
    writer.initialize(
        output_dir="_out_boxes",
        rgb=True,
        bounding_box_2d_tight=True,
        semantic_segmentation=True,
    )
    writer.attach([render_product])

rep.orchestrator.run()
simulation_app.close()

Each frame produces an RGB image plus annotation files. The `semantics` label attached to the cubes is what makes them appear in bounding boxes and segmentation masks.

| Data source | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|-------------|-----------|------------|
| Real, hand-labeled | Matches deployment conditions exactly | Slow and costly to label; rare cases are hard to capture |
| Synthetic (Replicator) | Perfect labels, unlimited variation, rare cases on demand | Sim-to-real gap in appearance and sensor noise |
| Mixed | Synthetic breadth plus real-world grounding | Requires careful dataset balancing and validation |

- Mismatched ROS 2 environments. Isaac Sim and your nodes must agree on ROS distribution, RMW implementation, and `ROS_DOMAIN_ID`, or topics silently fail to appear.
- Sim time mismatch. Nodes with `use_sim_time` set to true block or behave strangely if `/clock` is not published. Publish the clock from Isaac Sim and set `use_sim_time` consistently on every node.
- Broken TF tree. VSLAM publishes `map` to `odom` to `base_link`; if another node also publishes `odom` to `base_link` (for example leg odometry), the transforms fight. Decide which node owns each transform.
- Unrectified images. Setting `rectified_images` to true while feeding raw images degrades tracking. Rectify upstream or tell the node the truth.
- Unsynchronized stereo. Left and right images with mismatched timestamps cause poor depth and tracking. Use hardware-synchronized cameras or confirm that simulated cameras render on the same tick.
- Copying launch files across releases. Parameter names change. Use `ros2 param list` on the running node to see what it actually accepts.
- Synthetic-only training. Models trained only on synthetic data often underperform on real images. Always validate on a real held-out set.

- Isaac ROS provides GPU-accelerated ROS 2 packages; NITROS keeps data on the GPU between NITROS-enabled composable nodes
- Isaac ROS Visual SLAM (cuVSLAM) estimates pose from stereo cameras with optional IMU fusion and publishes odometry and TF
- nvblox fuses depth and pose into TSDF and ESDF maps and can provide a costmap to Nav2
- The ROS 2 bridge in Isaac Sim publishes simulated sensors as ROS 2 topics through OmniGraph
- Replicator generates perfectly labeled synthetic data with domain randomization

The previous chapter gave the robot a pose estimate and a map. Navigation is the next layer: choosing a path to a goal and following it safely. For wheeled robots this is well understood, and Nav2 is the standard ROS 2 solution. Humanoids add a layer underneath: every velocity command from Nav2 must become footsteps, and every footstep must keep the robot balanced.

Nav2 examples assume ROS 2 Humble. Plugin naming changed in later distributions (some planner plugins switched from `package/Class` to `package::Class`), and parameters are added between releases. Check the Nav2 documentation for your distribution.

Nav2 is a set of lifecycle-managed servers coordinated by a behavior tree (BT). For a humanoid, its `cmd_vel` output feeds a locomotion controller rather than wheel motors.

- The planner server computes a global path on the global costmap.
- The controller server follows that path at a fixed rate using the local costmap, producing velocity commands.
- The behavior server provides recoveries such as spinning or backing up.
- The BT navigator ties these together; the default tree replans periodically and triggers recoveries on failure.

Costmaps are 2D grids where each cell holds a traversal cost, assembled from layers: a static layer from a saved map, obstacle and voxel layers from live laser or point-cloud data, and an inflation layer that adds a cost gradient around obstacles. With Isaac ROS, nvblox can also supply a costmap layer built from its ESDF (Chapter 2).

| Plugin | Type | Strengths | Considerations |
|--------|------|-----------|----------------|
| NavFn | Global planner | Simple, robust grid search | Ignores robot kinematics |
| Smac 2D | Global planner | Cost-aware grid search, good default | Ignores heading constraints |
| Smac Hybrid-A* / Lattice | Global planner | Kinematically feasible paths | More tuning, more compute |
| DWB | Controller | Highly configurable trajectory scoring | Many critics to tune |
| Regulated Pure Pursuit | Controller | Smooth path tracking, easy to tune | Limited dynamic obstacle handling |
| MPPI | Controller | Sampling-based predictive control, supports omnidirectional motion | Heavier compute; tune critics carefully |

        import math
    import rclpy
    from rclpy.action import ActionClient
    from rclpy.node import Node
    from nav2_msgs.action import NavigateToPose

    def main(x: float = 3.0, y: float = 1.5, yaw: float = 1.57):
        rclpy.init()
        node = Node("goal_sender")
        client = ActionClient(node, NavigateToPose, "navigate_to_pose")

        goal = NavigateToPose.Goal()
        goal.pose.header.frame_id = "map"
        goal.pose.header.stamp = node.get_clock().now().to_msg()
        goal.pose.pose.position.x, goal.pose.pose.position.y = x, y
        goal.pose.pose.orientation.z = math.sin(yaw / 2.0)   # yaw-only quaternion
        goal.pose.pose.orientation.w = math.cos(yaw / 2.0)

        client.wait_for_server()
        send_future = client.send_goal_async(
            goal, feedback_callback=lambda m: node.get_logger().info(
                f"Remaining: {m.feedback.distance_remaining:.2f} m"))
        rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(node, send_future)

handle = send_future.result()
        if not handle.accepted:
            node.get_logger().error("Goal rejected")
            return
        result_future = handle.get_result_async()
        rclpy.spin_until_future_complete(node, result_future)
        node.get_logger().info(f"Finished with status {result_future.result().status}")

Nav2 treats the robot as a body that accepts velocity commands. A humanoid satisfies that interface only through a locomotion controller that converts each `Twist` into footsteps and joint targets.

| Aspect | Wheeled base | Humanoid |
|--------|--------------|----------|
| Footprint | Fixed, rigid polygon | Changes every step; torso sways side to side |
| Velocity tracking | Nearly immediate | Delayed by the step cycle |
| Lateral motion | Only on holonomic bases | Possible by side-stepping, usually slower than forward |
| Stopping | Brake in place | Needs one or more steps to come to rest |
| Failure mode | Collision | Collision or fall |

Practical consequences for Nav2 configuration:

- Use a circular footprint enclosing the full sway envelope, and velocity limits the gait controller can actually track.
- Prefer controllers that support omnidirectional motion (such as MPPI with an omni model) so the robot can side-step in tight spaces.
- Standard 2D Nav2 does not plan footsteps or stairs. That needs a footstep planner or a terrain-aware learned policy below Nav2.

Each leg alternates between stance (foot on the ground, bearing weight) and swing (foot moving forward). The whole-body gait alternates between double support, when both feet are down and weight shifts to the leading foot, and single support, when one foot swings. Heel strike and toe off are the events that bound these phases.

chunks.text:
The Zero Moment Point (ZMP) is the point on the ground where the net moment of the contact forces has no horizontal component. For a flat-footed robot, a common stability criterion is that the ZMP must stay inside the support polygon, the convex hull of the feet in contact. If balance would require the ZMP outside that polygon, the foot starts to tip.

The Linear Inverted Pendulum Model (LIPM) reduces the robot to a point mass at constant height `z_c` balanced on a massless leg. Its horizontal dynamics are linear: `x_ddot = omega^2 * (x - p)`, with `omega = sqrt(g / z_c)`. Here `x` is the center of mass (CoM) position and `p` is the ZMP. The capture point `xi = x + x_dot / omega` is where the robot must step to come to rest. Centroidal models extend these ideas to the robot's full linear and angular momentum, but the LIPM captures the core intuition, and its linearity is why LIPM planners are fast enough for real-time replanning. The script below walks a LIPM forward using a capture-point stepping rule.


G = 9.81

def lipm_step(x0: float, v0: float, p: float, t: np.ndarray, omega: float):
    """Closed-form LIPM solution with the ZMP fixed at p."""
    dx = x0 - p
    x = p + dx  np.cosh(omega  t) + (v0 / omega)  np.sinh(omega  t)
    v = dx  omega  np.sinh(omega  t) + v0  np.cosh(omega * t)
    return x, v

def simulate_walk(step_length=0.3, step_time=0.5, z_c=0.9, n_steps=8, dt=0.01):
    omega = np.sqrt(G / z_c)
    # Offset between capture point and stance foot for a periodic gait
    b = step_length / (np.exp(omega * step_time) - 1.0)

    p = -b              # first stance foot slightly behind the CoM
    x, v = 0.0, 0.0     # start at rest; initial capture point = 0
    t = np.arange(0.0, step_time + 1e-9, dt)
    log = []

    for k in range(n_steps):
        xs, vs = lipm_step(x, v, p, t, omega)
        log.extend(zip(k  step_time + t, xs, vs, [p]  len(t)))
        x, v = xs[-1], vs[-1]
        xi = x + v / omega          # capture point at end of step
        p = xi - b                  # place next foot to keep a periodic gait

    return np.array(log)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    log = simulate_walk()
    for time, x, v, p in log[::25]:
        print(f"t={time:4.2f}s  CoM={x:5.2f} m  vel={v:4.2f} m/s  foot/ZMP={p:5.2f} m")
    print(f"Average speed: {(log[-1, 1] - log[0, 1]) / log[-1, 0]:.2f} m/s (target 0.60)")

After the first step each step covers the target distance in `step_time`; the printed average is a little below target because the robot starts from rest. Real controllers add a finite foot (so the ZMP can move within the sole), lateral dynamics, swing-leg trajectories, and whole-body control to track the CoM plan with real joints.

An increasingly common alternative to hand-designed balance controllers is a neural network policy trained with reinforcement learning in simulation. Isaac Lab, built on Isaac Sim, is NVIDIA's framework for this, running many robot copies in parallel on the GPU. A typical velocity-tracking task is defined by:

| Component | Typical contents |
|-----------|------------------|
| Observations | Base angular velocity, projected gravity, velocity command, joint positions and velocities, previous action |
| Actions | Offsets to joint position targets, tracked by low-level PD controllers |
| Rewards | Track commanded velocity; penalize torque, joint acceleration, action changes, falls; reward adequate foot air time |
| Randomization | Friction, payload mass, motor strength, external pushes, sensor noise |
| Curriculum | Terrain difficulty that increases as the policy improves |

Isaac Lab ships example humanoid velocity tasks and training scripts for libraries such as RSL-RL. Script locations and task names change between releases, so treat this as the shape of the command rather than an exact path:

# From the Isaac Lab repository root (check the docs for your release's paths)
./isaaclab.sh -p scripts/reinforcement_learning/rsl_rl/train.py \
    --task Isaac-Velocity-Rough-H1-v0 --headless

The trained policy fits under Nav2 naturally: Nav2's `cmd_vel` becomes the policy's velocity command. Moving to hardware (sim-to-real) depends heavily on randomization, accurate actuator models, and careful safety testing.

Robust avoidance for a humanoid is layered, each layer acting on a shorter time horizon:

1. Global planning routes around mapped obstacles.
2. Local control (MPPI, DWB) steers around obstacles in the local costmap.
3. Collision monitoring slows or stops the robot when something enters a safety zone; Nav2 provides `nav2_collision_monitor` for this.
4. Reactive balance in the locomotion controller handles contacts and pushes.

A minimal reactive speed limiter placed between Nav2 and the locomotion controller illustrates layer 3:


from rclpy.node import Node
from geometry_msgs.msg import Twist
from sensor_msgs.msg import LaserScan

class SpeedLimiter(Node):
    # Scale forward speed down as obstacles ahead get closer
    def __init__(self, stop_dist=0.5, slow_dist=1.2, fov_deg=60.0):
        super().__init__("speed_limiter")
        self.stop_dist, self.slow_dist = stop_dist, slow_dist
        self.half_fov = np.deg2rad(fov_deg) / 2.0
        self.min_front = float("inf")
        self.pub = self.create_publisher(Twist, "/cmd_vel", 10)
        self.create_subscription(LaserScan, "/scan", self.on_scan, 10)
        self.create_subscription(Twist, "/cmd_vel_nav", self.on_cmd, 10)

def on_scan(self, scan: LaserScan) -> None:
        angles = scan.angle_min + np.arange(len(scan.ranges)) * scan.angle_increment
        ranges = np.asarray(scan.ranges)
        front = (np.abs(angles) < self.half_fov) & np.isfinite(ranges)
        self.min_front = float(ranges[front].min()) if front.any() else float("inf")

    def on_cmd(self, cmd: Twist) -> None:
        span = self.slow_dist - self.stop_dist
        scale = np.clip((self.min_front - self.stop_dist) / span, 0.0, 1.0)
        if cmd.linear.x > 0.0:
            cmd.linear.x *= scale
        self.pub.publish(cmd)

Remap Nav2's controller output to `/cmd_vel_nav` so this node sits in the path. A humanoid needs distance to stop, so `stop_dist` must cover the steps required to come to rest.

- Footprint too small. The standing footprint ignores torso sway, causing shoulder and arm collisions in doorways.
- Velocity limits above what the gait tracks. Nav2 assumes commands are executed; if the walker lags, the controller oscillates. Measure tracking in simulation first.
- Obstacles only at ankle height. A 2D laser at foot level misses tables and shelves. Use voxel or nvblox layers covering the robot's full height.
- Mixed TF ownership. VSLAM, leg odometry, and Nav2 must agree on who publishes the `map`, `odom`, and `base_link` transforms.
- Deploying RL policies without safety layers. Always keep an independent stop mechanism and collision monitor around a learned policy.

- Isaac Lab trains locomotion policies with RL in parallel simulation, using rewards, randomization, and curricula
